topics.title: Animal groups
topics.intro: Scientists sort animals into groups: mammals, birds, fish, reptiles and amphibians. Each group has special features.
topics.teach: Explain how you know a dolphin is a mammal, not a fish.
topics.talk: At the zoo or in a book, ask {him} which group each animal belongs to.

head: Group
Look for
For example
rows: hair or fur; babies drink milk

topics.title: What animals eat
topics.intro: Carnivores eat meat, herbivores eat plants, and omnivores eat both. A food chain shows who eats whom.
topics.teach: Explain a food chain that starts with grass.
topics.talk: Ask {him} whether {she} is a carnivore, herbivore or omnivore.

visual.caption: A food chain. Each arrow means “is eaten by”. It always starts with a plant.

topics.title: My body and staying healthy
topics.intro: Our bodies need food, water, exercise, sleep and clean hands to stay healthy. Our five senses tell us about the world.
topics.teach: Explain why we wash our hands.
topics.talk: Ask {him} which sense {she} would least like to lose, and why.

topics.title: Growing up: life cycles
topics.intro: Animals grow and change. A caterpillar becomes a butterfly; frogspawn becomes a frog; babies become grown-ups.
topics.teach: Explain the life cycle of a butterfly.
topics.talk: Look at baby photos together and talk about how {she} has changed.

topics.title: Plants
topics.intro: Plants need water, light and warmth to grow. They have roots, a stem, leaves and often flowers.
topics.teach: Explain what roots do for a plant.
topics.talk: Grow a bean in a jar together and watch the roots appear.

topics.title: Habitats
topics.intro: A habitat is the home where an animal or plant lives. It gives them food, water and shelter.
topics.teach: Explain why a polar bear could not live in a desert.
topics.talk: Look under a log or stone together for minibeasts.

topics.title: Materials
topics.intro: Everything is made from materials: wood, metal, plastic, glass, rock, fabric. We choose materials because of what they are like.
topics.teach: Explain why windows are made of glass, not wood.
topics.talk: Ask {him} what {her} raincoat is made of and why.

topics.title: Seasons and weather
topics.intro: The year has four seasons: spring, summer, autumn and winter. Each brings different weather and different length days.
topics.teach: Explain how the trees change through the seasons.
topics.talk: Ask {him} what season it is and how {she} can tell.

visual.caption: Spring: March to May. Summer: June to August (the longest days). Autumn: September to November. Winter: December to February (the shortest days).

topics.title: Space: the Sun, Moon and planets
topics.intro: Earth is one of eight planets going round the Sun. The Moon goes round the Earth. Real space is even more amazing than space stories!
topics.teach: Explain why we have day and night.
topics.talk: Look at the Moon together on a clear night. What shape is it today?

topics.title: Continents and oceans
topics.intro: The world has seven continents (big areas of land) and five oceans. Let’s find them on the map.
topics.talk: Find where you live on a globe, then find Antarctica.

topics.title: The United Kingdom
topics.intro: The UK is made of four countries: England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. Each has a capital city.
topics.teach: Name the four countries of the UK and their capitals.
topics.talk: Ask {him} which country of the UK you live in.

topics.title: Maps, directions and places
topics.intro: North, south, east and west help us find our way. Hot places are near the Equator; cold places are near the North and South Poles.
topics.teach: Explain why it is cold at the North Pole.
topics.talk: Use a compass app to find north from your front door.

visual.caption: Going clockwise from north: north, east, south, west.

topics.title: Pushes, pulls and magnets
topics.intro: A force is a push or a pull. Racing cars slow down because of friction. Magnets can pull without even touching!
topics.teach: Explain why a toy car goes further on a smooth floor than on carpet.
topics.talk: Race toy cars down a ramp onto different floors.

head: Magnet ends
What happens
visual.caption: Opposite poles attract. The same poles repel.

topics.title: Rocks and fossils
topics.intro: Rocks are under our feet everywhere. Some hold fossils: the remains of plants and animals from millions of years ago, like dinosaurs!
topics.talk: Look for fossils on a beach or in a museum.

steps: Millions of years later, it is found
visual.caption: How most fossils form.

items.prompt: Is a whale a fish?

options.text: Yes: it lives in the sea
options.feedback: Living in the sea doesn’t make you a fish! Whales breathe air and feed their babies milk, so they are mammals.

items.explain: Whales and dolphins breathe air through a blowhole and feed their babies milk: they are mammals.

items.prompt: Which animal group has hair or fur and feeds its babies milk?
items.explain: Mammals have hair or fur and feed their babies milk. Humans are mammals!

items.prompt: Which animal group has feathers, wings and a beak?
items.explain: All birds have feathers and lay eggs. Not all birds can fly: penguins swim instead!

items.prompt: Which animal group lives in water, has scales and breathes with gills?
items.explain: Fish breathe underwater using gills.

items.prompt: Which animal group has dry, scaly skin and lays eggs on land?
items.explain: Snakes, lizards, crocodiles and tortoises are reptiles.

items.prompt: Frogs live in water when young and on land when grown up. Which group are they?
items.explain: Amphibians have smooth, damp skin. Frogs, toads and newts are amphibians.

items.prompt: Which group does a penguin belong to?

options.feedback: Penguins have feathers and lay eggs: birds!
They swim, but they have feathers and breathe air.

items.explain: Penguins are birds that swim instead of fly.

items.prompt: Which group does a crocodile belong to?

options.feedback: Crocodiles have dry, scaly skin and lay eggs on land: reptiles.
They breathe air.

items.explain: Crocodiles are reptiles, cousins of the dinosaurs.

items.prompt: A bat can fly. Which group does it belong to?
items.explain: Bats have fur and feed their babies milk: they are the only mammals that can truly fly.

items.prompt: How many legs does an insect have?
items.explain: All insects have 6 legs. Spiders have 8, so they are not insects!

items.prompt: An animal that eats only meat is called a…
items.explain: Lions, sharks and owls are carnivores.

items.prompt: An animal that eats only plants is called a…
items.explain: Cows, rabbits and elephants are herbivores. So are capybaras!

items.prompt: An animal that eats plants AND meat is called an…
items.explain: Bears, pigs and most humans are omnivores.

items.prompt: Put this food chain in order, starting with the plant.
items.explain: Grass is eaten by the rabbit; the rabbit is eaten by the fox. Food chains always start with a plant.

items.prompt: Put this sea food chain in order.
items.explain: Seaweed → fish → seal → polar bear.

items.prompt: What is at the start of every food chain?

options.feedback: Big animals come at the END. Plants make food from sunlight, so they come first.
Plants come first.

items.explain: Plants make their own food using sunlight, so every food chain starts with a plant.

items.prompt: Capybaras eat grass and water plants. What does that make them?
items.explain: Plant-eaters are herbivores.

items.prompt: How many main senses do we have?
items.explain: Sight, hearing, smell, taste and touch.

items.prompt: Which part of the body do we use to smell?
items.explain: We smell with our nose.

items.prompt: Which part of the body do we use to taste?
items.explain: Our tongue has taste buds.

items.prompt: Why should we wash our hands before eating?

options.text: To make our hands smell nice
options.feedback: Soap smells nice, but the real reason is germs.

options.text: So our hands are wet for eating
options.feedback: We dry them afterwards!

items.explain: Germs are too small to see. Soap and water wash them away.

items.prompt: Why is exercise good for us?

options.text: It keeps our heart and muscles strong
It makes us grow taller straight away
options.feedback: Exercise keeps us healthy and strong, but it doesn’t make us taller at once.

options.text: It means we never need to sleep
options.feedback: We still need sleep!

items.explain: Exercise makes the heart pump stronger and keeps muscles and bones healthy.

items.prompt: Which meal is the healthiest?

options.feedback: Too much sugar is bad for teeth and bodies.

options.text: A big bowl of only crisps
options.feedback: We need lots of different foods.

items.explain: A balanced diet has lots of different foods, including fruit and vegetables.

items.prompt: Which part of the body pumps blood all around it?
items.explain: Your heart is a muscle about the size of your fist.

items.prompt: Which parts of the body do we breathe with?
items.explain: Our lungs take in air so our body gets oxygen.

items.prompt: What is the name for all the bones in your body?
items.explain: Your skeleton holds you up and protects parts like your brain and heart.

items.prompt: Put the life cycle of a butterfly in order.
items.explain: Egg → caterpillar → chrysalis (pupa) → butterfly, which lays more eggs.

items.prompt: Put the life cycle of a frog in order.
items.explain: Frogspawn (eggs) → tadpole → froglet (with legs) → frog.

items.prompt: Put these stages of a human life in order.
items.explain: Baby → toddler → child → teenager → adult.

items.prompt: Put the life cycle of a chicken in order.
items.explain: Egg → chick → young chicken → hen, which lays eggs.

items.prompt: What is a baby frog called?
items.explain: Tadpoles live in water and breathe with gills, like fish.

items.prompt: What is a baby cow called?
items.explain: A baby cow is a calf. A baby horse is a foal; a baby sheep is a lamb.

items.prompt: What is the hard case a caterpillar turns into before it becomes a butterfly?
items.explain: Inside the chrysalis, the caterpillar changes completely.

items.prompt: Which part of a plant takes in water from the soil?
items.explain: Roots hold the plant in the ground and take in water.

items.prompt: Which part of a plant holds it up and carries water to the leaves?
items.explain: The stem is like a straw carrying water up the plant.

items.prompt: Which part of a plant uses sunlight to make food?
items.explain: Leaves catch sunlight and make food for the plant.

items.prompt: What do plants need to grow well?

options.feedback: Water isn’t enough: they need light and warmth too.
Plants grow badly in the dark and the cold.

items.explain: Plants need water, light and a suitable temperature.

items.prompt: What grows into a new plant?
items.explain: Seeds (and bulbs) grow into new plants.

items.prompt: What is a deciduous tree?

options.text: A tree that loses its leaves in autumn
A tree that keeps its leaves all year
options.feedback: That is an evergreen tree, like a pine.
All trees have roots.

items.explain: Oak and sycamore are deciduous. Pine and holly are evergreen.

items.prompt: A plant is left in a dark cupboard. What will happen?
items.answer: it will turn pale and weak
distractors: it will turn a brighter green
items.explain: Without light, plants cannot make food. They turn yellow and weak.

items.prompt: Which of these has NEVER been alive?

options.feedback: A dead leaf was once alive on a tree.
Wood came from a tree, which was alive.

items.explain: Rocks, metal and plastic have never been alive. Wood and leaves come from living things.

c.note: a dead leaf, a wooden spoon

items.prompt: Which animal is suited to a cold, icy habitat?
items.explain: Polar bears have thick fur and fat to keep warm.

items.prompt: Which animal is suited to a hot, dry desert?
items.explain: Camels can go a long time without water.

items.prompt: Which animal lives in the ocean habitat?
items.explain: Sharks live in the ocean.

items.prompt: Where would you find woodlice?
items.explain: Woodlice like dark, damp places. That is their microhabitat.

items.prompt: Which habitat is hot and wet, with tall trees and lots of rain?
items.explain: Rainforests have more kinds of animals and plants than any other habitat on land.

items.prompt: Capybaras live near rivers and lakes in South America. Why is that a good habitat for them?

options.text: They love swimming and water plants
They need lots of snow and ice
options.feedback: South America near rivers is warm.

options.text: They hunt fish in the water
options.feedback: Capybaras are herbivores: they eat plants.

items.explain: Capybaras are excellent swimmers and can hide underwater from danger.

items.prompt: Why are windows made of glass?
items.explain: Transparent means you can see through it.

items.prompt: Which property makes a raincoat useful?
items.explain: Waterproof materials don’t let water through.

items.prompt: Which material would make the best spoon for hot soup?
items.explain: Metal is strong and doesn’t melt in soup.

items.prompt: You can change the shape of modelling clay by squashing, bending, twisting and…
items.explain: Squash, bend, twist and stretch: four ways to change shape with forces.

items.prompt: Which is made of wood?

options.feedback: Windows are glass.
Coins are metal.

items.explain: Pencils, tables and doors are often wooden.

items.prompt: Which material is natural (not made by people)?
items.explain: Wood grows on trees. Plastic and glass are made by people.

items.prompt: Charles Macintosh invented a famous waterproof coat. What did he use to make the fabric waterproof?
items.explain: In 1823 he joined two layers of fabric with rubber. Raincoats are still called “macs”!

items.prompt: Put the seasons in order, starting with spring.
items.explain: Spring, summer, autumn, winter, then spring again.

visual.caption: Spring: March to May. Summer: June to August (the longest days). Autumn: September to November. Winter: December to February (the shortest days).

items.prompt: In which season are the days longest?
items.explain: In summer, the Sun rises early and sets late.

items.prompt: In which season do many trees lose their leaves?
items.explain: Leaves turn red, orange and yellow in autumn and fall.

items.prompt: Which months are winter in the UK?
items.explain: Winter is the coldest season, with the shortest days.

items.prompt: What do we measure temperature with?
items.explain: A thermometer measures how hot or cold it is.

items.prompt: Why should you never look straight at the Sun?

options.feedback: Some people do sneeze in bright light, but the real danger is eye damage.
The Sun won’t go out!

items.explain: The Sun is so bright it can damage eyes, even through sunglasses.

items.prompt: How many planets go round the Sun?
items.explain: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.

items.prompt: Put these planets in order, closest to the Sun first.
items.explain: My Very Easy Method Just Speeds Up Naming planets: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune.

visual.caption: The planets in order from the Sun: My Very Easy Method Just Speeds Up Naming planets.

items.prompt: Which is the biggest planet?
items.explain: Jupiter is so big that all the other planets could fit inside it.

items.prompt: Which planet is called the Red Planet?
items.explain: Mars is covered in red, rusty dust. Robots called rovers explore it.

items.prompt: Which planet has famous bright rings made of ice and rock?
items.explain: Saturn’s rings are made of billions of chunks of ice and rock.

items.prompt: What is the Sun?
items.explain: The Sun is a star: a giant ball of hot, glowing gas. It looks big because it is close.

items.prompt: Why do we have day and night?

options.text: The Sun switches off at night
options.feedback: The Sun keeps shining: it is our side of the Earth that turns away.

options.text: The Moon covers the Sun every night
options.feedback: That only happens in a rare eclipse.

items.explain: The Earth spins once every 24 hours. When our side faces the Sun, it is day.

items.prompt: What goes round the Earth?
items.explain: The Moon goes round the Earth about once a month.

items.prompt: What is a person who travels into space called?
items.explain: Astronaut means “star sailor”. Tim Peake was a British astronaut on the International Space Station.

items.prompt: What is the International Space Station?
distractors: a train station on the Moon
a bright star in the sky
items.explain: It goes all the way round the Earth about every 90 minutes!
Asia is the biggest continent.
Africa has deserts, rainforests and lions.
North America includes Canada and the USA.
South America has the Amazon rainforest.
Antarctica is the coldest place on Earth, covered in ice. Penguins live there.
Europe is where the UK is.
Oceania includes Australia, where kangaroos live. Some books call it Australia.
The Pacific is the biggest ocean.
The Atlantic lies between Europe and America.
The Indian Ocean is near India and Africa.
The Southern Ocean surrounds Antarctica.
The Arctic is the smallest ocean, at the top of the world.

items.prompt: How many continents are there?
items.explain: Asia, Africa, North America, South America, Antarctica, Europe and Oceania.
England is the biggest country in the UK.
items.choosePrompt: Which country of the UK is highlighted?

items.explain: Scotland is in the north, with mountains and lochs.
items.choosePrompt: Which country of the UK is highlighted?

items.explain: Wales is in the west. Its flag has a red dragon.
items.choosePrompt: Which country of the UK is highlighted?

items.explain: Northern Ireland is across the Irish Sea.
items.choosePrompt: Which country of the UK is highlighted?

items.explain: London is the capital of England.
Edinburgh is the capital of Scotland.
Cardiff is the capital of Wales.
Belfast is the capital of Northern Ireland.

items.prompt: What is the capital city of England?
items.explain: London is the capital of England.

items.prompt: What is the capital city of Scotland?
items.explain: Edinburgh is the capital of Scotland.

items.prompt: What is the capital city of Wales?
items.explain: Cardiff is the capital of Wales.

items.prompt: What is the capital city of Northern Ireland?
items.explain: Belfast is the capital of Northern Ireland.

items.prompt: Which sea lies between Great Britain and Ireland?
items.explain: The Irish Sea is to the west; the North Sea is to the east.

items.prompt: On most maps, which direction is at the top?
items.explain: North is at the top; south at the bottom; east on the right; west on the left.

items.prompt: Which saying helps you remember the compass points going clockwise from north?
items.explain: North, East, South, West.

visual.caption: Going clockwise from north: north, east, south, west.

items.prompt: What is the imaginary line around the middle of the Earth called?
items.explain: Places near the Equator are hot all year.

items.prompt: Why is it cold at the North and South Poles?

options.text: The Sun’s light is weak and spread out there
They are the furthest from the Moon
options.feedback: The Moon doesn’t heat the Earth.

options.text: The snow there makes the cold
options.feedback: Snow is there because it is cold, not the other way round.

items.explain: Sunlight is weaker at the Poles, so they stay icy.

items.prompt: Which of these is a PHYSICAL feature (made by nature)?

options.feedback: A factory is made by people: a human feature.
Shops are human features.

items.explain: Physical features: mountain, river, beach, cliff. Human features: house, road, factory, port.

items.prompt: Which of these is a HUMAN feature (made by people)?

options.feedback: Rivers are natural: physical features.
Forests grow naturally.

items.explain: Bridges, roads and towns are human features.

items.prompt: Land with water all the way round it is called an…
items.explain: Great Britain is an island.

items.prompt: A force is a push or a…
items.explain: Kicking a ball is a push; opening a drawer is a pull.

items.prompt: Why does a toy car stop sooner on carpet than on a smooth floor?

options.text: There is more friction on carpet
Carpet is much heavier than floors
options.feedback: It is about grip: rough carpet rubs against the wheels more.

options.text: The car gets tired on carpet
options.feedback: Cars don’t get tired!

items.explain: Friction is a force that slows things down when surfaces rub together. Rough surfaces have more friction.

items.prompt: Which of these does a magnet pick up?
distractors: a paper clip made of plastic
items.explain: Magnets attract iron and steel. They don’t attract plastic, wood or most other metals.

items.prompt: What happens when you push the north poles of two magnets together?

options.feedback: Opposite poles attract. The SAME poles repel.
You can feel them pushing!

items.explain: Opposite poles attract; like poles repel.

items.prompt: A race car rolls down a ramp. How can you make it go further?

options.feedback: Colour doesn’t change the force.
A sticky floor adds friction, so the car stops sooner.

items.explain: A higher ramp gives the car more speed at the bottom.

items.prompt: What is a fossil?
items.answer: old remains of a living thing, turned to rock
distractors: a shiny jewel found in caves
a type of very old volcano
a kind of soil found by rivers
items.explain: Fossils form over millions of years.

items.prompt: Which young woman found amazing fossils on the beach at Lyme Regis about 200 years ago?
items.explain: When she was only about 12, Mary Anning found the skeleton of an ichthyosaur, a sea reptile. Later she found the first nearly complete plesiosaur skeleton.

items.prompt: How do most fossils form?

options.text: An animal is buried and slowly turns to rock
Animals turn to stone when they get cold
options.feedback: It takes burial and millions of years, not cold.

options.text: People carve them out of stone
options.feedback: Fossils are natural.

items.explain: Bones are buried in mud or sand; over millions of years the layers become rock.

steps: Millions of years later, it is found

items.prompt: What is soil made of?
items.answer: bits of rock and rotted plants
items.explain: Soil is broken rock plus rotting leaves, which feed plants.

items.prompt: How do we know dinosaurs existed?
items.explain: No people lived at the same time as dinosaurs. Fossils are our evidence.
